title: Why better education and health outcomes start with getting the basics right
gist: Cambodia has near-universal primary enrollment (97%) and 94% patient satisfaction yet Grade 6 students answer under half a basic math exam and only 3% of health centers offer the full service package; the gap traces to a 2.2%-of-income education budget, salaries absorbing 63-80% of frontline spending, and budget rules that keep money from reaching schools and clinics.

insights.claim: Cambodia has reached 97 percent net primary school enrollment, life expectancy above 70 years and 94 percent patient satisfaction, yet the average Grade 6 student answers less than half of a basic math exam.
insights.so_what: Access metrics are exhausted as a growth story; human-capital quality is the binding constraint on Cambodia's future workforce.
insights.quote: Access has raced ahead but outcomes have not kept up.
insights.locator: More Cambodian children are in school than ever
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Only 3 percent of Cambodian health centers offer the complete required package of services, although most deliver most of it.
insights.so_what: Service-completeness, not facility count, is the gap — implies procurement demand for equipment, medicines and staffing rather than new buildings.
insights.quote: Only 3 percent of health centers offer the complete required package of services
insights.locator: Similarly in the health sector, understaffing affects
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: The diagnosis rests on two new World Bank reports: a health service delivery survey of 288 public and private facilities across 11 provinces, and an education report tracing six public finance and human resource bottlenecks to learning.
insights.so_what: Names the primary-source evidence base for anyone underwriting Cambodian human-capital or health-sector programs.
insights.locator: Two new World Bank reports seek to explain
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Cambodia spends only about 2.2 percent of national income on education, less than half the average for countries at its income level, and this resource gap is a real binding constraint rather than a management problem.
insights.so_what: Under-spending at this scale caps learning outcomes regardless of reform quality — a fiscal-space story to watch in budget cycles.
insights.quote: Cambodia spends only about 2.2 percent of its national income on education, less than half the average for countries at its income level.
insights.locator: The resource gap is a real binding constraint
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Cambodian families cover roughly 59 percent of total education spending, a burden falling hardest on the poorest households.
insights.so_what: Majority-private financing of a public good signals both regressive incidence and a sizable private education/tutoring market.
insights.quote: covering roughly 59 percent of education spending
insights.locator: Families fill much of the gap
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Salaries now absorb 70 to 80 percent of Cambodia's education budget while capital spending fell from 21 percent of ministry spending in 2018 to just 6 percent in 2022, even as the system runs short of more than 16,000 classrooms.
insights.so_what: A crowded-out capital budget against a 16,000-classroom shortfall implies a large deferred school-construction pipeline.
insights.quote: capital spending fell from 21 percent of ministry spending in 2018 to just 6 percent in 2022
insights.locator: Moreover, salaries now absorb 70 to 80 percent
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Cambodian health centers put 63 percent of their resources into salaries, leaving little for the medicines, equipment and repairs that determine whether a service can actually be delivered.
insights.so_what: Same salary-heavy distortion as education — non-salary recurrent spend is the constrained line item across both sectors.
insights.locator: Frontline health budgets are similarly tilted
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Many Cambodian teachers have not fully mastered the content or teaching methods they are expected to use, and about one-fifth have received only minimal training; even though stronger graduates are now entering the profession, classroom practice has yet to improve.
insights.so_what: Better teacher intake alone does not lift learning — watch in-service training and practice reform, not recruitment stats.
insights.quote: Although stronger graduates are entering the profession, classroom practice has yet to improve
insights.locator: Weak outcomes often reflect gaps in the basics
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Textbook shortages persist in rural and remote Cambodian schools even though students with their own textbooks learn significantly more, and students who fall behind rarely receive effective remedial support.
insights.so_what: A low-cost, high-return input gap — textbook and learning-materials procurement is the cheapest lever on measured learning.
insights.locator: Students who fall behind rarely receive effective remedial support
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Understaffing affects 88 percent of Cambodian referral hospitals and 65 percent of health centers, and most health centers operate without a doctor at all.
insights.so_what: Structural clinical-workforce shortfall caps any service-expansion plan; medical training and task-shifting become priorities.
insights.quote: understaffing affects 88 percent of referral hospitals and 65 percent of health centers
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Electricity cuts hit more than half of Cambodian health centers, fewer than one in ten has a working generator, and stockouts of everyday medicines remain common.
insights.so_what: Concrete demand signal for backup power, cold chain and pharmaceutical supply-chain fixes in Cambodian primary care.
insights.quote: Electricity cuts hit more than half of health centers, fewer than one in ten has a working generator
insights.locator: Electricity cuts hit more than half of health centers
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Management and governance reform cannot substitute for missing physical and human basics — improving oversight around absent medicines, materials, staff and power will not deliver outcomes.
insights.so_what: A sequencing rule for development spend: fund inputs first, then systems — reverse order wastes both.
insights.quote: These are the holes in the hull, and tidying the management around them will not help if the basics are missing.
insights.locator: These are the holes in the hull
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

themes.theme: Why money fails to reach the frontline

insights.claim: Rigid rules on Cambodian schools' operating grants and an underused textbook tracking system directly prevent schools from buying the textbooks and remedial materials that learning depends on.
insights.so_what: Identifies a procurement-rule bottleneck: the constraint is spending authority, not only budget size.
insights.locator: Why resources don't reach the frontline
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Frontline budgeting in Cambodia is fragmented, with 79 percent of health centers and 81 percent of referral hospitals managing separate budgets by funding source, while schools cannot carry unspent balances into the next year.
insights.so_what: Fragmented, non-carryover budgets guarantee misallocation — a public financial management reform target with measurable payoff.
insights.quote: 79 percent of health centers and 81 percent of referral hospitals manage separate budgets by funding sources
insights.locator: Other constraints are shared across both sectors
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Cambodian spending rules reward year-end disbursement over strategic use, and frontline managers have little discretion to fill staffing gaps or move resources to where they are needed.
insights.so_what: Explains why higher budgets would not automatically improve outcomes — execution incentives are misaligned.
insights.quote: Spending rules reward year-end disbursement over strategic use
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Performance is rarely linked to financing in Cambodia, staff are unevenly distributed, and parallel data systems do not talk to each other, leaving managers without a clear picture.
insights.so_what: Points to results-based financing and data-system integration as the next reform wave — and a market for interoperable public-sector IT.
insights.locator: Performance is rarely linked to financing
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

themes.theme: Reform must move from finance ministry into sectors

insights.claim: Cambodia's Ministry of Economy and Finance has driven a respected reform program modernizing budgeting and building the core financial management system, but the next phase depends on the health and education ministries owning reform inside their own systems.
insights.so_what: Central-agency PFM wins have plateaued; execution risk now sits with line ministries — watch whether they link financial data to the central system.
insights.locator: Reform must now move into sectors
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs

insights.claim: Turning Cambodian access into real learning and care is framed as an investment in the future workforce that supports long-term job creation and economic growth.
insights.so_what: Links service-delivery quality to Cambodia's labor productivity trajectory — relevant to manufacturing-upgrade and FDI theses.
insights.locator: Cambodia has already brought millions of children into school
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
